reconcile.connective: Traditional commentators read the ch. 1 grant as implicitly subject to the ch. 2 exception — the later restriction narrows, but does not contradict, the earlier provision.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells (Skeptic's Annotated Bible) lists this as a genuine conflict, arguing that Genesis 1:29 grants all seed-bearing plants and fruit trees without qualification, while Genesis 2:17 then forbids one tree — creating an inconsistency in the divine grant.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: and every tree, in which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; all but the tree of knowledge, of good and evil, afterwards excepted
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill reads the Genesis 1:29 grant as already carrying an implicit qualification — 'all but' the tree excepted in ch. 2 — directly addressing how the broad ch. 1 provision and the ch. 2 restriction cohere.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: a very generous, large, and liberal allowance this… even of any, and every tree in the garden, excepting one, next forbidden.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill's comment on Gen 2:16 frames the command as confirmation of the breadth of the grant with the single exception appended — explicitly reconciling the two passages by treating the ch. 2 command as expansive, not restrictive relative to ch. 1.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the relation of the Genesis 1 food grant to the Genesis 2 prohibition under the harmonizing tradition that the later exception narrows rather than contradicts the earlier provision.
